title: Bloom's Two Sigma Problem (1984)
explainer: In a 1984 Educational Researcher paper, Benjamin Bloom reported that students who received one-on-one tutoring with mastery learning scored, on average, about two standard deviations higher than students taught conventionally in a classroom - meaning the typical tutored student outperformed roughly 98% of the untutored group. Bloom posed this as a genuine problem: tutoring works dramatically better than group instruction, but doesn't scale, which is the exact tension anyone doing one-on-one mentoring in tech is implicitly exploiting and should understand the size and limits of.

title: Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development
explainer: Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky, in work from the last years of his life in the early 1930s, described the 'zone of proximal development' - the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help from a more knowledgeable other. The practical technique built on this idea, later named 'scaffolding' by Jerome Bruner and colleagues, is to give a mentee a task just past their current ability and support them through it, then withdraw that support as they become capable - which is a precise description of what good technical mentoring is actually doing moment to moment.
